I am 47 years old and have farmed in Quzhou County all my life. Around here, the land is flat and fertile, and the climate suits the wheat–maize double-cropping system. I have about 8 mu of contracted land, and I am not going to gamble with new crops because the grain stations and local traders buy wheat and maize reliably. My winter wheat went into the ground last October after rotary tillage. I used an improved semi-dwarf variety and sowed about 30 jin per mu. Now that spring has arrived, the wheat is greening up. I will irrigate three or four times in total this wheat season—once before jointing, once at booting, and once at grain filling if the weather stays dry. For fertilizer, I already put down compound fertilizer as basal last autumn, and now I will topdress with urea at jointing. Altogether that gives roughly 45 kg of nitrogen, 20 kg of phosphorus, and 5 kg of potassium per mu. I will spray pesticides four times: herbicide early, then fungicide and insecticide as the weather warms.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant hybrid maize—everyone here uses no-tillage seeders that drill straight into the wheat stubble. Hybrid seed yields higher and resists lodging better. Maize needs less water, so two irrigations will do—one at the V6 stage and one at tasselling. I will apply compound fertilizer at sowing and sidedress with urea later, totaling about 25 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 6 kg potassium per mu. Three pesticide applications should handle weeds and the corn borer. I expect about 1,000 kg of wheat and 1,100 kg of maize per mu. This is the safe, proven way to feed my family and earn steady cash.
